title: Empress Dowager Cixi and the Guangxu Emperor
text:
Cixi began as a concubine of the Xianfeng emperor of the Qing dynasty and became powerful as the mother of his only son. When that son, the Tongzhi emperor, died young in January 1875, without an heir, Cixi chose the next emperor herself. She picked her three-year-old nephew Zaitian, son of her own sister and an imperial prince. Choosing a small child, rather than an adult of the next generation, allowed her to go on ruling as regent.

The boy, who reigned as the Guangxu emperor, was taken from his parents and raised in the palace under her authority. He was taught to call her his royal father. He grew up nervous and sickly but intelligent, and keen on reform.

In 1889 Cixi formally handed power to him, though she kept a close watch. In 1898, after China's defeat by Japan, Guangxu launched a burst of reforms known as the Hundred Days. Conservative officials turned to Cixi. In September 1898 she took back control, executed several reformers and confined the emperor to a pavilion on an island in the palace lake. He remained a virtual prisoner for the rest of his life.

On 14 November 1908, Guangxu died at thirty-seven. Cixi died the following day. In 2008 scientific tests on his remains found a lethal dose of arsenic, suggesting that he was poisoned.
lesson: When family ties and power become entangled, a guardian can become a jailer. Raising a child to need us is not the same as raising them.
location: Forbidden City and Zhongnanhai, Beijing, China
source: Jung Chang, Empress Dowager Cixi (2013); Qing court records; Chinese forensic report on the Guangxu emperor's remains (2008)
caveat: Who ordered the poisoning is unknown; suspects include Cixi and court officials.
